316046.title: Carmichael's totient function conjecture
316046.statement:
For a positive integer $n$ let

$$
\varphi(n) = \#\{k : 1 \le k \le n,\ \gcd(k,n) = 1\}
$$

be Euler's totient function, and for a positive integer $f$ let

$$
A(f) = \#\{n \ge 1 : \varphi(n) = f\}
$$

be the multiplicity of $f$ as a value of $\varphi$.

For every integer $n \ge 1$ there exists an integer $m \ne n$, $m \ge 1$, with

$$
\varphi(m) = \varphi(n).
$$

Equivalently, $A(f) \ne 1$ for every positive integer
$f$; that is, no value attained by $\varphi$ is attained by exactly one
argument.
316046.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Totient multiplicity: every n needs a distinct positive partner. Bounded partner search passes. General inverse-totient multiplicity-one obstruction remains.

316050.title: Grimm's conjecture
316050.statement:
For positive integers $n$ and $k$, if the $k$ consecutive integers $n+1, n+2,
\dots,
n+k$ are all composite, then there exists a sequence of distinct prime numbers $\left(p_{i}\right)_{i=1}^{k}$
such that $p_{i}$ divides $n+i$ for every $1 \leq i \leq k$.

A weaker assertion: for positive integers $n$ and $k$, if no prime lies in the
interval $[n+1, n+k]$, then

$$
\prod_{1\,\leq\,x\,\leq\,k}(n+x)
$$

has at least $k$ distinct prime divisors.
316050.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Prime-factor matching on every composite interval. Hall matching passes on all maximal composite runs in [2,10000], hence their subintervals. No all-interval Hall inequality established.

search_coverage.space: all composite intervals contained in [2,10000], via maximal-run prime-factor bipartite matching

316055.title: Newman's conjecture
316055.statement:
For a nonnegative integer $n$, let $p(n)$ denote the number of partitions of
$n$, i.e. the number of ways of writing $n$ as a sum of positive integers
without regard to order, with the convention $p(0)=1$, so that

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} p(n)q^{n} = \prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1-q^{k}}.
$$

For every integer $m \ge 1$ and every integer $r$ with $0 \le r \le m-1$, the
set

$$
\{\, n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \;:\; p(n) \equiv r \pmod{m} \,\}
$$

is infinite.
316055.assessment_and_remaining_gap: For each modulus and residue, infinitely many partition values are required. Every residue appears in the finite sample; this does not test infinitude. Later-work lead: 2025 paper for moduli with at least two prime divisors; body unread.

316056.title: Scholz conjecture
316056.statement:
For a positive integer $x$, an addition chain for $x$ is a finite sequence of
positive integers

$$
a_0 = 1,\; a_1,\; a_2,\; \dots,\; a_r = x
$$

such that for every $k$ with $1 \le k \le r$ there exist indices $i, j$ with $0
\le i, j \le k-1$ (possibly $i = j$) satisfying $a_k = a_i +
a_j$. The length of such a chain is $r$, the number of sums performed, and
$l(x)$ denotes the least length of an addition chain for $x$, i.e.

$$
l(x) = \min\{r : \text{there is an addition chain } 1 = a_0, a_1, \dots, a_r = x\}.
$$

For every integer $n \ge 1$,

$$
l(2^n - 1) \le n - 1 + l(n).
$$
316056.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Exact addition-chain lengths through n=8 satisfy Scholz. Sorting a useful positive addition chain gives an increasing chain, so search normalization is sound. No all-n Mersenne chain construction.

search_coverage.space: all increasing addition chains needed for exact l(n),l(2^n-1), 1<=n<=8

316057.title: Singmaster's conjecture
316057.statement:
For an integer $a>1$, let

$$
N(a)=\#\left\{(n,k)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{2}\;:\;0\le k\le n,\ \binom{n}{k}=a\right\},
$$

the number of positions in Pascal's triangle at which the entry equals
$a$ (each occurrence in a row being counted separately, so that e.g. $\binom{n}{k}$
and $\binom{n}{n-k}$ count as two occurrences when $k\neq
n-k$). Note that $N(a)$ is finite for every $a>1$, since $\binom{n}{k}=a$ forces
$n\le a$.

There exists a natural number $M$ such that

$$
N(a)\le M\qquad\text{for all integers } a>1;
$$

equivalently, $N(a)=O(1)$.
316057.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Existence of a uniform multiplicity bound cannot be refuted by one finite Pascal box. Recorded multiplicity is truncated; no global N(a) claim.

search_coverage.kind: bounded sample cannot refute existence of uniform constant

316077.title: Kummer–Vandiver conjecture
316077.statement:
Let $p$ be an odd prime, let $\zeta_p$ be a primitive $p$-th root of unity, and
let

$$
K = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)^{+} = \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p + \zeta_p^{-1})
$$

be the maximal real subfield of the
$p$-th cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Let
$h_K$ denote the class number of $K$, i.e. the order of the ideal class group of
the ring of integers of $K$; equivalently, $h_K =
h_2$ is the second factor in the decomposition $h = h_1
h_2$ of the class number $h$ of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$, where $h_2 =
h_K$ and $h_1 = h/h_K$.

Then

$$
p \nmid h_K
$$

for every odd prime $p$.
316077.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Exact maximal-real-cyclotomic class numbers were not computed. No executable class-group implementation/primary algorithm bridge established; zero finite-search coverage. This is an explicit unmet part of the requested early-search pass.

316111.title: Pillai's conjecture
316111.statement:
Call an integer $p$ a perfect power if $p = x^n$ for some integers $x \ge
1$ and $n \ge 2$, and let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 <
\cdots$ be the increasing enumeration of the perfect powers $\ge 1$. Then

$$
\lim_{k \to \infty} (p_{k+1} - p_k) = \infty;
$$

equivalently, every positive integer is representable in only finitely many ways
as a difference of two perfect powers. More generally, for all fixed positive
integers $A$, $B$, $C$, the set of quadruples $(x, y, m, n)$ of integers with

$$
x \ge 1, \quad y \ge 1, \quad m \ge 2, \quad n \ge 2, \quad (m,n) \neq (2,2),
$$

satisfying

$$
A x^n - B y^m = C
$$

is finite.
316111.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Perfect-power VALUE gaps sampled. The generalized quadruple wording allows x=1 and arbitrarily many n in some fixed equations, an excluded representation/domain defect; it does not settle the intended Pillai conjecture. No gap-divergence proof.

search_coverage.space: all perfect-power VALUES <=1000000; exponents<=19 suffice for base>=2
search_coverage.kind: gap sample cannot refute limit; base=1 representation defect excluded

316114.title: Agoh–Giuga conjecture
316114.statement:
Let the Bernoulli numbers $B_k \in \mathbb{Q}$ be defined by

$$
\frac{t}{e^{t}-1}=\sum_{k\ge 0}B_{k}\frac{t^{k}}{k!}.
$$

For an integer $p>1$ the rational number $pB_{p-1}$ has denominator prime to
$p$, so the congruence $pB_{p-1}\equiv -1 \pmod
p$ is meaningful, meaning that the numerator of $pB_{p-1}+1$ written in lowest
terms is divisible by $p$.

For every integer $p>1$,

$$
p \text{ is prime} \iff pB_{p-1}\equiv -1 \pmod{p},
$$

and equivalently, for every integer $p>1$,

$$
p \text{ is prime} \iff \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} i^{\,p-1}\equiv -1 \pmod{p}.
$$
316114.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Direct power-sum version checked for all n<=2000. This does not prove the Bernoulli equivalence; no formal bridge or all-composite exclusion proved.

316115.title: Agrawal's conjecture
316115.statement:
Let $n$ and $r$ be positive integers with $\gcd(n,r)=1$, and consider the
congruence

$$
(X-1)^{n}\equiv X^{n}-1 \pmod{n,\;X^{r}-1},
$$

meaning that the two polynomials $(X-1)^{n}$ and $X^{n}-1$ have the same image
in the ring
$(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})[X]/(X^{r}-1)$, i.e. every coefficient of $(X-1)^{n}-(X^{n}-1)$,
after reduction of exponents modulo $r$ via $X^{r}=1$, is divisible by $n$.

For every such pair $(n,r)$ satisfying this congruence, either $n$ is prime or

$$
n^{2}\equiv 1 \pmod{r}.
$$
316115.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Primary AKS conjecture recovered as cyclic polynomial congruence; exact all-pairs search n<=2000,r<=40 has no witness. Heuristic counterexample framework of Lenstra-Pomerance is not a construction. Need composite n and admissible r with n^2!=1 mod r.

search_coverage.space: all 2<=n<=2000, 2<=r<=40; gcd=1 pairs; skip prime n and n^2=1 mod r since conclusion already true
search_coverage.arithmetic: exact cyclic convolution via carry-free Kronecker substitution; diagnostic, not a Lean certificate

316121.title: Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture
316121.statement:
Call a positive integer $m$ *powerful* if for every prime $p$ with $p \mid m$
one also has $p^{2} \mid m$; equivalently, $m$ is powerful if and only if $m =
a^{2}b^{3}$ for some positive integers $a,
b$. Writing the prime factorization as $m=\prod_i
p_i^{\alpha_i}$, this says that $\alpha_i \geq 2$ for every $i$.

For every integer $n \geq 1$, the three consecutive integers $n$, $n+1$,
$n+2$ are not all powerful; that is, there is no $n \geq
1$ such that each of $n$, $n+1$, $n+2$ satisfies the condition that every prime
dividing it divides it at least twice.
316121.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Powerful means every nonzero prime exponent>=2, with 1 vacuously powerful. Complete sieve range gives no triple. This is far below known computational work; no novelty.

search_coverage.space: all 1<=n<=999998; powerful membership by prime exponents

316122.title: Feit–Thompson conjecture
316122.statement:
For distinct primes $p$ and $q$, set

$$
N_{p,q} \;=\; \frac{p^{q}-1}{p-1} \;=\; 1 + p + p^{2} + \cdots + p^{q-1}, \qquad N_{q,p} \;=\; \frac{q^{p}-1}{q-1} \;=\; 1 + q + q^{2} + \cdots + q^{p-1},
$$

both of which are positive integers. Then for every pair of distinct primes
$p$ and $q$,

$$
\frac{p^{q}-1}{p-1} \;\nmid\; \frac{q^{p}-1}{q-1};
$$

that is, there exists no integer $k$ with $N_{q,p} = k\,N_{p,q}$.
316122.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Tested ordered distinct prime pairs <=100 for divisibility of cyclotomic quotients. The famous p=17,q=3313 common-factor example refutes a stronger coprimality claim, not this divisibility claim.

316130.title: New Mersenne conjecture
316130.statement:
For an odd natural number $p$ consider the following three conditions:

(i) there is a natural number $k$ such that $p = 2^k + 1$, $p = 2^k - 1$, $p =
4^k + 3$, or $p = 4^k - 3$;

(ii) $2^p - 1$ is prime;

(iii) $(2^p + 1)/3$ is prime (note that $3 \mid 2^p + 1$ for every odd $p$, so
this quotient is an integer).

For every odd natural number
$p$, if at least two of the conditions (i), (ii), (iii) hold for $p$, then all
three hold for $p$.

316142.title: Bing–Borsuk conjecture
316142.statement:
For a metric space $M$, say that $M$ is *homogeneous* if for any two points
$m_1,m_2\in M$ there is a homeomorphism of $M$ onto itself taking $m_1$ to
$m_2$.

Say that a metric space
$M$ is an *absolute neighborhood retract* (ANR) if for every closed embedding $f:M\rightarrow
N$ into a metric space $N$ there exists an open neighbourhood $U$ of $f(M)$ in
$N$ that retracts onto $f(M)$, i.e. there is a continuous map
$r:U\rightarrow f(M)$ with $r\restriction f(M)=\mathrm{id}_{f(M)}$.

Say that $M$ is an *$n$-manifold* if every point of
$M$ has an open neighbourhood homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $n\geq 1$ and let
$M$ be a metric space which is homogeneous, is an ANR, and has topological dimension $\dim
M=n$. Then $M$ is an $n$-manifold.
316142.assessment_and_remaining_gap: Homogeneous finite-dimensional metric ANR manifold recognition. Seminar claims of higher-dimensional counterexamples surfaced, but full construction body not acquired. Do not report those claims as verified resolutions.

316143.title: Borel conjecture
316143.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be closed topological manifolds that are aspherical, i.e.
connected with $\pi_n(M)=\pi_n(N)=0$ for all $n\ge 2$ (equivalently, with
contractible universal covers). Then every homotopy equivalence

$$
f\colon M\to N
$$

is homotopic to a homeomorphism.

In particular, if $M$ and $N$ are closed aspherical topological manifolds with
$\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(N)$, then $M$ and $N$ are homeomorphic.

316154.title: Torsion conjecture
316154.statement:
For a number field $K$ and an abelian variety $A$ over $K$, let $A(K)$ denote
the group of $K$-rational points of $A$ and let

$$
A(K)_{\mathrm{tors}} = \{P \in A(K) : nP = 0 \text{ for some integer } n \ge 1\}
$$

be its torsion subgroup, which is finite since $A(K)$ is a finitely generated
abelian group.

For every pair of integers $g \ge 1$ and $d \ge 1$ there exists a constant
$C(g,d) < \infty$ such that

$$
\#A(K)_{\mathrm{tors}} \le C(g,d)
$$

for every number field $K$ with $[K:\mathbb{Q}] =
d$ and every abelian variety $A$ over $K$ with $\dim A =
g$; that is, the bound depends only on $g$ and on the degree
$d$, and not otherwise on $A$ or on $K$.
